query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A W-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a tailored microstructure (e.g., SCCPs structure) can deliver enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward hydrogen evolution (HER) and oxidation (HOR) reactions compared to conventional catalysts.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized tungsten-based refractory HEA exhibiting a stable microstructure (e.g., coherent δ-lamellae with embedded nano-precipitates)
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to standard electrochemical HER and HOR conditions (e.g., in an acidic electrolyte such as 0.5 M H2SO4) and perform cyclic voltammetry and durability cycling tests
generation.conditions: Room temperature operation in acidic media with controlled potential windows matching typical HER/HOR testing protocols
generation.structural_mediator: The robust multi-element matrix with tungsten sites and fine-scale microstructural features (e.g., δ-lamellae, dispersed precipitates) that are expected to provide active sites for hydrogen adsorption and enhance resistance to structural degradation
generation.mechanism: The unique d-electron configuration of tungsten combined with the synergistic effects from other refractory elements in the HEA is hypothesized to improve electron transfer kinetics. Meanwhile, the microstructural stability, as evidenced by the SCCPs structure, is anticipated to maintain catalytic performance over long-term operation by resisting dissolution and morphological changes under harsh electrochemical environments
generation.predicted_outcome: The W-based refractory HEA is predicted to exhibit lower overpotentials and improved stability (i.e., minimal degradation in catalytic activity over extended cycling) compared to conventional catalysts (e.g., Pt or monometallic tungsten-based catalysts)
generation.baseline: Catalytic performance metrics from conventional Pt-based catalysts and simple tungsten catalysts under similar HER/HOR test conditions
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions relevant to laboratory scale HER/HOR testing (acidic media, room temperature, standard potential windows). Extreme pH conditions, very high temperatures, or significantly different electrolyte compositions may fall outside the validated parameter space
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanical and thermal robustness of tungsten-based HEAs is well supported in high-temperature and high-stress environments, direct evidence of their electrochemical catalytic performance toward HER and HOR remains limited. The optimal alloy composition and surface modification required for maximizing catalytic activity are uncertain and would need further systematic study

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the tungsten-based refractory HEA with a well-characterized SCCPs microstructure and test them in a standard three-electrode electrochemical cell in 0.5 M H2SO4. Compare HER and HOR activity (overpotentials, Tafel slopes) and stability (activity after prolonged cycling) with benchmark Pt-based catalysts. Include control experiments with conventional tungsten-based materials.
measurements: Overpotential at a set current density (e.g., 10 mA cm−2)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for charge transfer resistance
Cyclic voltammetry stability tests over 10,000 cycles
Post-test structural analysis (TEM/SEM) to evaluate microstructural integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the W-based refractory HEA does not exhibit a significantly lower overpotential, improved Tafel slopes, and maintained catalytic performance after durability cycling (comparable or inferior relative to conventional Pt-based catalysts), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

The NbMoTaW HEA was fabricated with mixed multi-element powders. The powders of Nb (99.9%), Mo (99.9%), Ta (99.9%), and W (99.9%) were weighed with nominal composition in equal atomic percent, respectively. The shapes of powder grains were spherical or near-spherical. The particles were mixed with a mass ratio m w : m Ta : m Mo : m Nb of 184:181:96:93, and the powders were then mechanically milled in a KQM-X/B planetary ball mill for 2 h and dried at 45 °C for 8 h.

In the experiment, the SLM process was conducted using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a P L (Maximum power of laser) of 500 W fiber laser in a protective atmosphere of argon with an amount of oxygen under 20 ppm. The substrate was C45 steel plate with a size of 50 mm× 50 mm × 20 mm. The fabricated sample model was a cuboid with a size around 10 mm × 10 mm × 0.5 mm.

The main parameters of the SLM process are laser scanning velocity ( v ), hatch distance ( ds ), layer thickness ( dz ), laser power factor ( f p ), and laser spot diameter ( d L ).
